mechanism: What it is: Crystal methamphetamine is a synthetic stimulant. The "crystal" form is methamphetamine hydrochloride, usually smoked, snorted, injected, or swallowed.
How it works in the brain and body:

Dopamine surge: It forces nerve cells to release huge amounts of dopamine, the brain chemical linked to reward, motivation, and pleasure. It also blocks dopamine from being reabsorbed. Result = intense euphoria and energy.
Norepinephrine and serotonin: It also increases norepinephrine = alertness, heart rate, blood pressure go up. And serotonin = mood changes.
Neurotoxicity: At high doses it can damage dopamine and serotonin neurons. The brain becomes less able to produce these chemicals naturally over time.
Duration: Effects can last 8-12 hours when smoked, longer if taken other ways, because it stays in the system and keeps releasing neurotransmitters.
demographics: Patterns vary a lot by country and year. Globally, research and health agencies report use across:
Age: Most commonly reported in adults 18-40, but can occur in teens and older adults.
Gender: Reported in both men and women. Some studies show higher rates among men, but gap is narrowing in some regions.
Socioeconomic: Reported across income levels. In some areas it’s linked to joblessness, long work hours, or areas with limited treatment access.

Geography: Use is documented in North America, parts of Asia, Australia, and is monitored in Southern Africa including Zimbabwe and South Africa. Police and health data track seizures and treatment admissions.
Occupation: Reported among some groups with shift work or who feel pressure to stay awake, though most users are not in any single job type.
Note: Data is often incomplete because use is under-reported and illegal in most places.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys and treatment data include:
Energy and wakefulness: To stay awake for work, school, or long shifts.
Euphoria: The dopamine surge creates intense pleasure and confidence at first.
Appetite suppression and weight loss: Some use it to reduce hunger.
Mood effects: Short-term relief from depression, boredom, or stress for some users.
Social factors: Peer influence, availability, and low cost relative to other stimulants in some markets.
Performance pressure: Belief it helps with focus or productivity, though effects reverse with regular use.
Most people who start do not intend long-term dependence, but the brain changes make stopping hard.
effects: Increased heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature
Reduced dopamine function = anhedonia, depression, memory problems
Damage to neurons that use dopamine and serotonin
Psychosis symptoms in some: paranoia, hallucinations, delusions
Increased risk of stroke and seizures
"Meth mouth": severe dental decay, gum disease
Increased risk of infectious diseases, especially if injected and needles are shared
Withdrawal: Fatigue, depression, increased appetite, strong cravings
healthImpact: Acute risks: Overdose can cause hyperthermia, cardiac arrest, stroke, seizures. Risk goes up with higher doses and mixing with other drugs.
Chronic disease: Cardiovascular disease, dental disease, skin infections, mental health disorders.
Mental health: Higher rates of anxiety, depression, psychosis. Can trigger underlying mental health conditions.
Pregnancy: Use during pregnancy is linked to low birth weight, preterm birth, and developmental problems. Talk to an OBGYN immediately if pregnant and using.

Treatment: There is no FDA/WHO approved medication specifically for meth dependence. Treatment is usually behavioral therapy, counseling, and support groups. Medical care treats physical complications.
socialImpact: Individual: Job loss, school dropout, relationship breakdown, financial problems due to cost and time spent obtaining/using.
Family: Increased conflict, child neglect, domestic violence in some households.
Community: Linked to crime, including theft and violence. Strains health services, emergency rooms, and law enforcement.
Stigma: Users often face stigma which can make them avoid seeking healthcare.
Economic: Costs to healthcare systems, policing, and lost productivity. In countries with associations like transport operators, substance use can also affect workplace safety and licensing.
Public health: Injection use can spread HIV and Hepatitis B/C if equipment is shared.
harmReduction: If use is happening, key health steps are:
Talk to a healthcare professional. They can check heart, dental, and mental health.
Avoid sharing needles or other equipment to reduce infection risk.
Stay hydrated, eat, and try to sleep to reduce acute harm.
Support services: Look for addiction counselors, rehab centers, or community health programs. In Zimbabwe, public clinics and hospitals can refer to mental health and substance use services.
If you think someone is in immediate danger from overdose, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts, seek emergency medical help right away.

mechanism: What it is:
Cannabis = plant Cannabis sativa. Main active chemicals = cannabinoids.
THC - tetrahydrocannabinol: the main "high" chemical. Skunk = high-THC strain, often 15-25% THC.
CBD - cannabidiol: non-intoxicating. May reduce anxiety, inflammation.
Other 100+ cannabinoids + terpenes affect smell, taste, and effects.
How it works in brain and body:
Endocannabinoid system ECS: Your body naturally makes chemicals like anandamide that bind to CB1 and CB2 receptors.
CB1 receptors: Mostly in brain. THC binds to them and mimics natural chemicals but much stronger.
Result in brain:
Dopamine release = euphoria, reward
Changes glutamate and GABA = altered perception, memory, time sense
Affects hippocampus = short-term memory issues
Affects cerebellum = coordination issues
CB2 receptors: Mostly in immune system and organs = inflammation and pain modulation.
Onset:
Smoked/vaped: 1-5 min, peak 30 min, lasts 2-4 hours
Edibles: 30-120 min, peak 3-4 hours, lasts 6-8 hours
Metabolism: Liver breaks down THC → 11-OH-THC → stored in fat. Can show in urine for weeks.
Tolerance: Daily use = brain makes fewer CB1 receptors. Need more for same effect.
demographics: Based on WHO, UNODC, and regional surveys:
Age: Most common 18-35. University students and young workers highest. Teen use 15-19 also reported.
Gender: Historically higher in males. Gap is closing. Women report using more for anxiety, pain, sleep.
Geography: Used globally. In Zimbabwe and Southern Africa: called "mbanje" or "dagga". Traditional use + recreational use. Skunk = potent strains imported or grown locally.
Income: Ranges from cheap street mbanje to expensive skunk and edibles. Used across all income levels.
Context: Social with friends, alone to relax, for creativity, music, pain management, sleep.
Legal status: Legal for medical/recreational in some countries. Illegal in Zimbabwe except licensed medical/industrial. This affects how people access and talk about it.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys and research:
Relaxation and stress relief: #1 reason. "It helps me switch off".
Pain and medical: Chronic pain, arthritis, menstrual cramps, chemotherapy nausea. CBD used for anxiety and epilepsy in some medical settings.
Sleep: Many use at night for insomnia.
Euphoria and fun: Social use, music, parties. Skunk used for stronger effect.
Creativity: Artists, musicians report it helps ideas flow.
Appetite: "Munchies" - used by people with low appetite.
Peer and culture: Social circles, normalization, music and media.
Alternative to alcohol/pills: Some switch to avoid hangovers or side effects.
Most people start for fun or relief. Some develop regular use patterns.
effects: Euphoria, relaxation, altered sense of time
Anxiety or paranoia at high THC doses, especially skunk
Adolescent brain: Regular use before age 25 linked to lower IQ, attention problems. Brain still developing.
Mental health: Can trigger psychosis in people with risk. High-THC skunk linked to higher anxiety and psychosis risk.
Dependence: ∼9% of users develop Cannabis Use Disorder. Withdrawal: irritability, insomnia, low appetite, cravings.
Motivation: "Amotivational syndrome" debated, but heavy daily use linked to low drive.
Lungs: Smoking causes bronchitis, cough. Vaping/edibles avoid this.
Heart: Temporary increased heart rate and BP. Risk for people with heart disease.
Hormones: May affect testosterone and fertility with heavy use.
Pregnancy: Linked to low birth weight. Not recommended.
healthImpact: Acute risks: Car accidents due to impaired driving. Anxiety/panic attacks. Rare: cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome = severe vomiting with chronic use.
Chronic risks: Lung irritation if smoked. Mental health effects in vulnerable people. Dependence.
Benefits: Medical cannabis approved in some countries for chronic pain, epilepsy, chemo nausea, MS spasticity. CBD oil used for some childhood epilepsy.
Skunk risk: Higher THC = higher risk of anxiety, paranoia, psychosis compared to lower-THC mbanje.
Treatment: Behavioral therapy, support groups. No FDA-approved medication for cannabis withdrawal yet.
Harm reduction: Don’t drive. Don’t mix with alcohol. Start low, go slow with edibles. Avoid high-THC if prone to anxiety.
socialImpact: Individual: Money spent, school/work performance if used heavily. Legal trouble where illegal.
Family: Conflict if use is secret or problematic. Parenting issues if dependent.
Community: Law enforcement costs in places where illegal. Healthcare costs for cannabis-related ER visits.
Economy: Legal markets generate tax and jobs in some countries. Illicit market still big where banned.
Culture: Music, art, and language around mbanje in Southern Africa. "Mbanje" often stigmatized but also normalized in some groups.
Policy: Debate between criminalization vs medicalization vs legalization. Affects stigma and access to treatment.
Stigma: Can prevent people from seeking help. Medical users may face judgment.
harmReduction: If using: avoid driving, avoid mixing with alcohol/other drugs.
If under 25, brain is still developing = higher risk.
If you have history of psychosis or severe anxiety, high-THC skunk may worsen it.
Talk to a healthcare professional for medical questions or if you want to cut down.
In Zimbabwe, ask at a clinic for referral to counseling services.
If someone has severe anxiety, paranoia, or chest pain after use, seek medical help.

mechanism: What it is:
Combustible tobacco = burning dried tobacco leaves and inhaling the smoke. Includes cigarettes, cigars, shisha/hookah, pipe tobacco, hand-rolled.
Key chemicals + how they work:
Chemical	Mechanism in Body/Brain
Nicotine	Binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in brain. Causes dopamine + norepinephrine release = pleasure, alertness, appetite suppression. Highly addictive.
Carbon Monoxide CO	Binds to hemoglobin better than oxygen. Reduces oxygen to heart, brain, muscles.
Tar	Sticky mix of 7000+ chemicals. Sticks to lungs. Contains 70+ carcinogens.
Oxidants + Free Radicals	Damage cells and DNA.
Other: Benzene, formaldehyde, arsenic, lead	Carcinogens and toxins
How it works:
Inhalation: Smoke goes to lungs → nicotine in blood in 10 seconds → brain in 7 seconds.
Brain reward: Dopamine spike in reward pathway = "buzz", relief, focus.
Stimulation then sedation: Low dose = stimulant. Higher dose = relaxation.
Tolerance: Brain makes more receptors. Need more nicotine for same effect.
Dependence: Physical + psychological. Withdrawal starts 2-3 hours after last cigarette.
Shisha difference: 1 hour session = smoke from 100+ cigarettes. Water cools smoke but does NOT filter toxins. Charcoal adds CO.
demographics: Based on WHO, CDC, and Zimbabwe STEPS survey:
Age: Most start 15-24. Regular use peaks 25-44. Shisha popular 16-30.
Gender: Globally men smoke more. In Zimbabwe: ∼30% of men, ∼2% of women smoke cigarettes. Shisha use more equal by gender, seen as "social".
Geography: 1.3 billion smokers worldwide. In Africa: cigarettes rising, shisha growing in cities. Zimbabwe: cigarettes common, shisha in bars/clubs, cigars for special occasions.
Income: Cigarettes used across all incomes. Cheap brands + single sticks common in low-income areas. Shisha and cigars more middle/upper income.
Context:
Cigarettes: Stress relief, breaks, habit, social
Shisha: Group activity in cafes, seen as "cultural" or "safer than cigarettes"
Cigars: Status, celebration, not inhaled by some users
Occupation: Higher rates in manual labor, hospitality, military, transport.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys:
Addiction: Nicotine dependence. Most adult smokers started as teens.
Stress and mood: "It calms me down". Nicotine relieves withdrawal anxiety.
Weight control: Appetite suppression.
Social: Smoke breaks, peer groups. Shisha = "let’s chill at the hookah lounge".
Perception: Cigars = luxury. Shisha = flavored, "not as bad" as cigarettes.
Marketing: Tobacco industry targets youth with flavors, sleek packaging. Shisha marketed with fruit flavors.
Habit: Associated with coffee, alcohol, after meals, driving.
effects: Strong dependence. Withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, low mood, cravings, trouble concentrating
Lungs: COPD, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, lung cancer
Heart: Heart attack, stroke, peripheral artery disease. CO damages vessels.
Cancer: Lung, throat, mouth, bladder, kidney, pancreas, stomach
Other: Impotence, fertility problems, gum disease, tooth loss, cataracts, osteoporosis
Pregnancy: Miscarriage, low birth weight, SIDS
Shisha/Cigars: Same risks. 1 shisha session = 1.7kg of smoke vs 0.5-1g from 1 cigarette. Cigar smoke has higher nitrosamines.
healthImpact: Death: WHO: 8 million deaths/year from tobacco. 7 million from direct use, 1.2 million from secondhand smoke.
Disease burden: #1 preventable cause of death. Major cause of NCDs.
Secondhand smoke: Causes lung cancer and heart disease in non-smokers. Children get asthma, ear infections.
Thirdhand smoke: Residue on clothes, furniture.
Healthcare costs: Huge burden on hospitals, especially for COPD and cancer.
Treatment for quitting: Works. Nicotine replacement therapy NRT, varenicline, bupropion, counseling. Quitting at any age helps. After 1 year: heart disease risk cut in half.
Shisha myth: "Water filters it" = false. Same toxins + more CO.
socialImpact: Individual: Money. 1 pack/day = $1000+/year. Time lost on smoke breaks.
Family: Secondhand smoke harms kids and partners. Money spent on tobacco vs food/school.
Workplace: Sick days, lower productivity, fire risk.
Community: Litter, fires. Shisha lounges create social spaces but also health risks.
Economy: Tobacco industry = jobs and tax. But healthcare costs and lost productivity cost more.
Stigma: Smoking increasingly stigmatized. Bans in public places.
Youth: Shisha flavors and social media make it look "safe and fun" to teens.
harmReduction: There is no safe level of combustible tobacco. "Light" cigarettes are not safer.
Shisha is not a safe alternative.
Quitting helps at any age. Talk to a doctor about NRT or medication.
Avoid secondhand smoke. Don’t smoke around kids/pregnant people.
In Zimbabwe: visit your local clinic. WHO and Ministry of Health run quit programs.
If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or coughing blood, see a healthcare professional immediately.

mechanism: What they are:
Vapes / e-cigarettes = battery-powered devices that heat a liquid "e-liquid" or "juice" into an aerosol you inhale. No burning like cigarettes.
Main components in e-liquid:
Ingredient	Mechanism
Nicotine	Same as cigarettes. Binds to nicotinic receptors → dopamine release = pleasure, focus, addiction
Propylene Glycol PG + Vegetable Glycerin VG	Base liquids. When heated they create the visible "vapor" aerosol
Flavorings	7000+ flavors. Some like diacetyl, cinnamaldehyde may irritate lungs when inhaled
Other: THC, CBD, synthetic cannabinoids	In some "vape" products, especially illicit ones
How it works:
Battery heats coil → liquid turns to aerosol in 1-3 seconds
Inhalation: Aerosol goes to lungs → nicotine in blood in 10-20 seconds → brain in 10 seconds
Nicotine salts: Newer devices use "nic salts" which are smoother, so you can inhale higher nicotine 20-50mg/mL without harshness = faster dependence
No combustion: Because there’s no burning, there’s no tar and less carbon monoxide vs cigarettes. But aerosol still has chemicals, metals from coil, and ultrafine particles.
Tolerance + dependence: Same as cigarettes. Brain adapts, needs more for same effect.
Device types: Disposable vapes, pod systems like Juul, refillable tanks, "mods". Heat-not-burn products are similar but heat tobacco instead of liquid.
demographics: Based on WHO, CDC, and youth surveys:
Age: Biggest group = 16-30 year olds. Teen use 13-17 rose sharply 2018-2022 globally due to flavors and disposables.
Gender: Slightly more male users, but female use rising fast, especially with flavored disposables.
Geography: Used worldwide. Highest in US, UK, Europe. Growing in Africa including Zimbabwe, mainly in cities and universities. Sold in shops, online, at clubs.
Income: Disposables $5-$15. Refillable systems cheaper long-term. Marketed as "modern" and "cleaner".
User types:
Smokers switching: Adults trying to quit cigarettes
Dual users: Smoke + vape
Never-smokers: Teens/young adults starting with vapes due to flavors
Context: Seen as tech, social, and "discreet" because vapor dissipates fast and smells like fruit.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys:
Quit smoking: #1 reason adults give. Perceived as less harmful than cigarettes.
Nicotine without smoke: Get nicotine buzz without tar, ash, smell.
Flavors: Mango, mint, dessert flavors. Makes it appealing to new users.
Social and image: Seen as trendy, "clean", tech. Easy to use in places where smoking is banned.
Cost: In long term cheaper than packs of cigarettes.
Control: Can choose nicotine level 0mg to 50mg, and adjust vapor.
Stress and habit: Hand-to-mouth habit + nicotine relieves withdrawal.
For teens, top reasons = flavors, peer use, curiosity, and "it’s not smoking".
effects: Nicotine buzz: alertness, focus, mild euphoria
Reduced withdrawal if you’re a smoker
Anxiety, irritability if you go too long without
Addiction: Nicotine is highly addictive. Nic salts make it easier.
Adolescent brain: Use before age 25 linked to attention, learning, and mood issues. Nicotine affects brain development.
Withdrawal: Cravings, irritability, trouble concentrating, low mood
Lungs: Irritation, cough. EVALI = "e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury" linked to vitamin E acetate in illicit THC vapes. Long-term lung effects still being studied.
Heart: Nicotine increases heart rate and BP. May increase risk of heart disease over time.
Oral: Gum disease, dry mouth, tooth decay from sugar in some juices
Chemicals: Aerosol contains formaldehyde, acrolein, metals like nickel, lead from coils
Compared to cigarettes: Public Health England and UK NHS say vaping is ∼95% less harmful than smoking because no combustion. But "less harmful" ≠ "safe". For never-smokers, any risk is added risk.
healthImpact: Acute: Nicotine poisoning if liquid ingested. Battery explosions rare but serious. EVALI outbreak 2019 mainly from illicit THC vapes.
Chronic: Still being studied because vaping only popular since ∼2010. Known risks: nicotine dependence, lung irritation. Potential long-term risks to heart and lungs.
Youth: Biggest concern. Nicotine addiction + brain development + gateway to cigarettes for some teens.
Pregnancy: Nicotine can harm fetal development. Not recommended.
Secondhand aerosol: Contains nicotine and particulates, but much less than cigarette smoke.
Treatment: Behavioral support, NRT. Some doctors use vaping as a smoking cessation tool in adults.
socialImpact: Individual: Money spent on devices and pods. Addiction can be strong with high-nic disposables.
Family: Parents concerned about teen use. "Hidden" because easy to conceal.
School/Work: Vaping in bathrooms, classrooms. Schools spending on detectors.
Community: Litter from disposables = plastic + battery waste. Environmental issue.
Marketing: Flavors and influencers target youth. Social media shows "cloud chasing" and tricks.
Regulation: Many countries restrict flavors, age 18+/21+, advertising. Zimbabwe regulates under tobacco laws.
Debate: Harm reduction tool for smokers vs risk of new generation getting addicted to nicotine.
harmReduction: If you don’t smoke, don’t start vaping.
If you smoke and switch, it’s likely less harmful, but best is to quit nicotine entirely.
Avoid illicit THC vapes and unknown liquids.
Don’t share devices due to infection risk.
Talk to a healthcare professional for help quitting. NRT, counseling works.
If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or severe cough after vaping, seek medical care.

mechanism: What it is:
Snuff = powdered or finely ground tobacco. "Bute" is the common name in Zimbabwe and Southern Africa.
There are 2 main types:
Dry snuff: Fine powder inhaled through the nose
Moist snuff: Placed between gum and cheek/lip. Also called "oral snuff" or "chewing tobacco" in some places
Key chemicals + how they work:
Chemical	Mechanism

Nicotine	Absorbed through nose lining or mouth mucosa. Goes to blood in 30-60 sec → brain in 10 sec. Binds nicotinic receptors → dopamine release = pleasure, alertness, appetite suppression. Highly addictive.
TSNAs - Tobacco Specific Nitrosamines	Carcinogens formed during curing and fermentation. Major cancer risk.
pH adjusters: Lime, ash, bicarbonate	Make nicotine more "freebase" so it absorbs faster.
Flavorings: Menthol, fruit, clove	Mask harshness, make it easier to use.
How it works:
Absorption: No burning. Nicotine absorbed through mucous membranes. Slower peak than cigarettes but lasts longer 30-60 min.
Brain reward: Dopamine in reward pathway = buzz, relief, focus.
No combustion: Means no carbon monoxide, no tar from smoke. But still has carcinogens from tobacco itself.
Tolerance + dependence: Same as cigarettes. Brain makes more receptors. Withdrawal = irritability, cravings.
demographics: Based on WHO, CDC, and African tobacco surveys:
Age: Most start 15-30. Common in adults 25-55. In some communities, elders use it daily.

Gender: In Southern Africa, snuff use is higher in women than cigarettes. In Zimbabwe: ∼5-8% of women and ∼10-15% of men report smokeless tobacco use. Globally varies: very high in India, Pakistan, South Africa, Zambia.
Geography: Used worldwide. "Bute" common in Zimbabwe, South Africa, Botswana, Malawi, Zambia. Also called "snuif" in Afrikaans areas.
Income: Cheap. A small tin costs $0.50-$2 and lasts days. Used across all income levels, especially rural areas.
Context:
Social: passed around, offered as greeting
Functional: "keeps me awake", "helps with headaches", "stops hunger"
Cultural: used in traditional ceremonies in some communities
Occupation: Farmers, drivers, security, people who can’t smoke at work.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys and ethnographic studies:
Nicotine addiction: Most users are dependent. Started as teens.
Discreet: No smoke, no smell. Can use at work, in church, at night.
Perceived as "safer" than smoking: No lungs involved, so people think it’s less harmful.
Traditional and cultural: Passed down in families. Gifted as sign of respect.
Functional: Reduces hunger, keeps people alert for driving or night work. Some use for toothache or "to clear sinuses".
Cost: Cheaper than cigarettes long term.
Availability: Sold at markets, tuck shops, bus stations. No age restriction enforcement in some areas.
effects: Dizziness or nausea for new users
Burning sensation in nose or mouth
Withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, headaches, trouble concentrating
Mouth: Gum recession, tooth loss, leukoplakia = white patches that can become cancer
Cancer: Oral cancer, throat cancer, esophageal cancer, pancreatic cancer. TSNAs are the main cause. Risk lower than smoking for lung cancer, but higher for mouth/throat.
Heart: Nicotine increases risk of heart disease and stroke
Pregnancy: Nicotine crosses placenta = low birth weight, miscarriage risk
Nose: Chronic irritation, nosebleeds with dry snuff
Note: Because there’s no smoke, risk of lung disease and COPD is much lower than cigarettes. Cancer risk shifts to mouth/throat/pancreas.
healthImpact: Cancer: IARC classifies smokeless tobacco as carcinogenic. Oral cancer rates higher in heavy users.
Cardiovascular: Nicotine contributes to hypertension and heart disease.
Dental: Major cause of gum disease and tooth loss in regular users.
Addiction: Same withdrawal as cigarettes. Can be hard to quit.
Secondhand: No secondhand smoke, but spit and residue can be an issue.
Treatment: Quitting helps. NRT, counseling, and support groups work. Because there’s no smoke, switching from cigarettes to snuff reduces some risks but adds others.
Children: Accidental ingestion of snuff can cause nicotine poisoning.
socialImpact: Individual: Money saved vs cigarettes. But dental costs and health costs later.
Family: Normalizes tobacco use for kids. Spitting can be unhygienic.
Community: Widely accepted in some cultures. Sold openly at markets.
Economy: Small local industry. No huge tax like cigarettes, but still revenue.
Stigma: Less stigma than smoking because no smoke. Sometimes seen as "old people’s habit".
Regulation: WHO FCTC includes smokeless tobacco. Some countries ban flavors or require cancer warnings on tins. In Zimbabwe it’s sold legally but with health warnings.
Public health: Often left out of tobacco control programs that focus on smoking. Need targeted education.
harmReduction: There is no safe tobacco product. Snuff has lower lung risk but higher mouth cancer risk.
Don’t use while pregnant.
Check mouth regularly for white patches or sores. See a dentist/doctor.
If you want to quit: talk to a clinic. NRT gum/patch can help with cravings.
Keep away from children due to poisoning risk.
If you have a sore in mouth that doesn’t heal in 2 weeks, lumps, or trouble swallowing, see a healthcare professional.

mechanism: What it is:
LSD = lysergic acid diethylamide. Semi-synthetic compound made from ergot fungus. Active in micrograms. Common doses: 50-200 µg.
How it works in the brain:
5-HT2A serotonin receptor agonist: Main mechanism. LSD binds strongly to serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, especially in the cortex.
Glutamate surge: Activating 5-HT2A increases glutamate in key brain areas. This disrupts normal communication between brain networks.
Default Mode Network DMN disruption: DMN = "ego" network. LSD reduces DMN activity = "ego dissolution", feeling connected to everything.
Sensory cortex changes: Visual cortex becomes more active even with eyes closed = visuals, patterns, colors.
Other receptors: Also hits dopamine D2, adrenergic, and other serotonin receptors. This adds to mood and perception changes.
Onset: Oral = 30-60 min. Peak = 3-4 hours. Total duration = 8-12 hours. No physical withdrawal because no dependence develops.
Tolerance: Builds fast. Using 2 days in a row = second dose barely works. Resets in ∼7-14 days.
demographics: Based on WHO, UNODC, and survey data:
Age: Most common 18-30. University students and young adults. Use drops after 35.
Gender: Historically more men, ∼2:1 ratio. Gap narrowing.
Geography: Used globally. More common in North America, Europe, Australia. Reported in cities in Africa including Zimbabwe but much less common than alcohol or cannabis due to cost and availability.
Income: Not tied to income. Used across classes. Often obtained through social networks, not street dealers.
Context:
Recreational: Music festivals, with friends, "tripping"
Therapeutic research: Clinical trials for depression, anxiety, PTSD, addiction
Spiritual: Some use for self-exploration, "meaning making"
Form: Usually on blotter paper, liquid, or microdots.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from research and user surveys:
Altered perception and experience: Visuals, music enhancement, time distortion. Described as "beautiful" or "mind-blowing".
Self-exploration: To understand self, emotions, trauma. "Therapeutic" use without a doctor.
Spiritual: Feelings of unity, transcendence, connection to nature.
Creativity: Artists and musicians report new ideas.
Curiosity: "I want to see what it’s like".
Mental health: Some use hoping for antidepressant effects. Clinical research is testing LSD and psilocybin for depression, but this is NOT self-medication.
Most people do not use daily. It’s usually occasional due to long duration and tolerance.
effects: Perceptual: Visual patterns, colors brighter, trails, synesthesia "hearing colors"
Cognitive: Time feels slow/fast, thoughts loop, insights or confusion
Emotional: Euphoria, wonder, or anxiety/panic "bad trip"
Ego: Sense of self may dissolve
Increased heart rate, blood pressure, body temp
HPPD - Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder: Rare. Flashbacks, visual snow weeks/months later.
Psychosis risk: Can trigger lasting psychosis in people with schizophrenia risk.
No physical dependence and very low addiction potential. Brain doesn’t adapt like with nicotine or opioids.
Potential benefits: Research shows 1-2 guided doses may help depression, anxiety, addiction. Still experimental.
No organ toxicity at normal doses. LSD is not physically toxic.
Risk is mainly psychological and from unsafe behavior during trip.
healthImpact: Acute risks:
"Bad trip": Panic, paranoia, can lead to self-harm
Accidents: Poor judgment, impaired coordination
Adulterants: LSD is often not what’s sold. NBOMe and other chemicals are dangerous and have caused deaths.
Chronic risks: HPPD, triggering mental illness in vulnerable people.
Contraindications: History of psychosis, bipolar, severe anxiety. Also dangerous with lithium, some antidepressants.
Medical research: Phase 2/3 trials for LSD-assisted therapy for anxiety and depression. Not approved yet except in research.
Treatment: No overdose antidote needed. Care is supportive: "talk down", safe environment. Benzos sometimes used for severe panic.
Legal: Schedule I in most countries. Possession = criminal offense.
socialImpact: Individual: Can lead to positive life changes for some, or psychological distress for others. Time off work/school during trip.
Family: Misunderstanding and stigma. Parents may not understand use.
Community: Associated with 1960s counterculture, music, art. Today: festivals, online forums.
Healthcare: ER visits mainly for panic and accidents, not overdose.
Policy: Decriminalization movements in some US cities and countries for personal use. Research being funded again after 40-year ban.
Stigma: Seen as "dangerous drug" vs "tool for consciousness" depending on culture.
Economy: Black market only where illegal. No big industry.
harmReduction: Set and Setting: Mindset + safe environment greatly affect outcome.
Don’t use alone. Have a sober "trip sitter".
Test substances. Many "LSD" blotters are actually NBOMe which can be lethal.
Avoid if: You have mental illness history, are pregnant, or taking medications.
Don’t drive or operate machines for 24 hours.
If someone is panicking: Stay calm, reassure, safe quiet space. Seek medical help if they are a danger.
Talk to a healthcare professional for mental health support.

mechanism: What they are:

Ultra-processed foods UPF: Foods made mostly from substances extracted from foods + additives. NOVA Group 4. Examples: packaged snacks, soft drinks, instant noodles, sweetened cereals, sausages, frozen meals. Usually 5+ ingredients you don’t cook with at home.
Sugar: Added sugars = sucrose, high-fructose corn syrup, glucose, etc added during processing. Not counting natural sugar in whole fruit.
How they work in the body and brain:
Sugar
Blood glucose spike: Sugar → glucose in blood in 15 min. Triggers insulin from pancreas.
Brain reward: Activates dopamine pathways like other rewards. Especially when combined with fat + salt.
Fructose metabolism: In liver. Excess fructose → fat in liver = fatty liver.
No satiety signal: Liquid sugar doesn’t trigger fullness well. Easy to over-consume.
Ultra-processed foods
Engineered for hyper-palatability: Perfect ratios of sugar + fat + salt + texture + flavor = brain says "eat more".
Fast digestion: Refined carbs + emulsifiers = spikes blood sugar fast.

Type 2 Diabetes: Insulin resistance from weight gain + liver fat
Heart disease: High BP, high triglycerides, inflammation
Fatty liver: Fructose → liver fat → NASH

Gut: Less fiber = poor gut bacteria, constipation

healthImpact: Global burden: WHO: diet is #1 risk factor for death. UPF and sugar major contributors.
NCDs: 70% of deaths now from NCDs: heart disease, diabetes, cancer, obesity.
Children: Early exposure = taste preference for life, obesity, dental problems.
Healthcare costs: Diabetes and heart disease treatment costs billions.

socialImpact: Individual: Money spent on food that doesn’t nourish. Health problems = missed work.

mechanism: What it is:
Gambling = risking money or something of value on an outcome based partly on chance.
Sports betting = wagering on sports results, live games, virtual games, odds.
How it works in the brain:
Dopamine reward system: The brain releases dopamine not just when you win, but when you anticipate a win. Near-misses trigger almost as much dopamine as wins.
Variable ratio reinforcement: You don’t win every time. This is the most addictive reward schedule. Same as social media likes. Brain keeps chasing "the next one".
Losses disguised as wins LDWs: Betting $10, "winning" $3 back. Brain registers it as a win even though you lost $7.
Cognitive distortions:
Illusion of control: "I have a system"
Gambler's fallacy: "I’m due for a win"
Availability bias: Remember big wins, forget losses
Stress hormones: Adrenaline, cortisol spike during bets = excitement. Crash after losses.
Online/mobile factor: 24/7 access, instant deposits, live in-play betting. Faster bets = faster dopamine loops.
Tolerance: Need to bet more money or take bigger risks for same "buzz".
demographics: Based on WHO, academic studies, and African gambling surveys:
Age: Peak 18-35. Young men highest risk. Teen gambling rising via mobile and esports.
Gender: Men bet more and more heavily. Women gambling growing, especially online casino and lottery.
Geography: Legal and widespread globally. In Zimbabwe: sports betting shops, USSD codes, and apps are common in cities. Also lottery, casino, and card games.
Income: Used across all incomes. Low-income groups often spend higher % of income. Marketed as "way out of poverty".
Occupation: Students, unemployed, transport workers, security. Anyone with mobile money access.
Context: Watching soccer, after work, with friends, during data bundles promos. Ads during sports matches.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys:
Money: Hope to win big, pay bills, escape poverty. "One big win will change my life".
Excitement: Adrenaline rush. Makes watching sports more interesting.
Social: Betting with friends, workplace pools, discussing odds.
Escape: To cope with stress, boredom, depression, unemployment.
Skill illusion: "I know soccer, so I can predict". Especially sports betting.
Marketing: Free bets, "deposit bonus", celebrity endorsements. Ads link betting to masculinity, success, "being a fan".
Accessibility: Mobile money + USSD means you can bet in 30 seconds from anywhere.
effects: Anxiety, irritability while waiting for results
Obsessive thinking about odds and "next bet"
Increased heart rate, sweating during bets
Gambling Disorder: Classified in DSM-5. Like addiction. Cravings, loss of control, chasing losses.
Depression and anxiety: From debt and shame
Suicidal thoughts: Higher rates in problem gamblers
Stress-related: High BP, ulcers, headaches, insomnia
Neglect: Skipping meals, hygiene, exercise to gamble
Substance use: Often co-occurs with alcohol to cope
healthImpact: Mental health: #1 impact. Depression, anxiety, addiction. Suicide risk 15x higher in problem gamblers.
Financial: Debt, loans, selling assets, borrowing. Leads to housing loss, inability to pay school fees.
Physical: Stress illnesses. No direct toxin like drugs, but health declines due to neglect.
Family health: Domestic conflict, child neglect when money goes to betting.
Treatment: Works. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy CBT, support groups like Gamblers Anonymous, financial counseling. No medication specifically for gambling.
Screening: Clinics can use 2-3 question screens: "Have you felt need to bet more? Have you lied about gambling?"
socialImpact: Individual: Job loss, legal problems from theft/fraud to fund gambling.
Family: #1 cause of financial conflict. Children go without food/school fees. Trust breakdown.
Community: Rise of betting shops in neighborhoods. Loan sharks. Crime to fund habit.
Economy: Gambling industry = jobs, tax revenue, sports sponsorships. But social costs: welfare, healthcare, policing often higher.
Sports: Match-fixing risk. Betting companies sponsor teams and leagues. Makes betting look "normal".
Culture: Normalization via ads during games. "If you don’t bet, you’re not a real fan" messaging.

harmReduction: Set limits: Time and money before you start. Use app deposit limits.
Don’t chase losses: Lost money is gone. Betting more rarely wins it back.
Track wins/losses: Most people underestimate how much they lose.
Take breaks: Don’t gamble when stressed, drunk, or depressed.
Talk to someone: Friends, counselor, clinic. Debt counseling helps.

Algorithms: Rank you based on activity, attractiveness score, location, preferences. Shows you people "likely" to match with you to keep you engaged.
Dopamine loop: Notification → match → chat → date. Each step gives a dopamine hit. Apps are designed to maximize time-on-app.
Gamification: Badges, boosts, "you have 5 new likes". Turns dating into a game.
Low friction: 30 seconds to make profile. Chat instantly. Meet same day. Removes traditional barriers.
Geolocation: Shows people near you. "Nearby" = more likely to meet.
Monetization: Free with ads + limits. Paid tiers: unlimited swipes, see who liked you, boost profile.

mechanism: What it is:
Cocaine is a stimulant derived from the coca plant. "Powder cocaine" = cocaine hydrochloride, usually snorted. "Crack cocaine" = freebase form, usually smoked.
How it works in the brain:
Dopamine reuptake block: Both forms block the dopamine transporter. Dopamine builds up in the synapse. This creates euphoria, increased energy, and reinforcement.
Norepinephrine and serotonin: Also blocked. Leads to increased alertness, heart rate, blood pressure, and mood changes.
Onset difference:
Powder: snorted = 3-5 min onset, lasts 15-30 min
Crack: smoked = 8-10 sec onset, lasts 5-10 min. The rapid onset makes it more addictive.
Tolerance: With repeated use the brain produces less dopamine naturally, so more drug is needed for the same effect.
demographics: Reported patterns vary by country and data source. Global monitoring agencies note use across:
Age: Most commonly 18-45 years. Some use reported in teens and older adults.
Gender: Historically higher in men, but use among women has increased in many regions.
Form differences: Powder cocaine more reported in higher-income groups in some countries. Crack more reported in areas with poverty and limited treatment access.
Geography: Cocaine use is documented in the Americas, Europe, and is monitored in parts of Africa including Southern Africa. Crack use is reported in urban centers globally.
Context: Reported among people in nightlife, some with shift work, and others facing stress, unemployment, or peer influence.
Data is often incomplete because use is illegal and under-reported.
whyPeopleUse: Reported reasons from surveys and treatment literature:
Euphoria and energy: Short intense high, increased confidence, talkativeness.
Performance: Belief it helps with focus, stamina, or social performance. Effects are short and followed by crash.
Appetite suppression: Used by some for weight control.
Social factors: Peer groups, availability, nightlife settings.
Coping: Short-term escape from stress, depression, or boredom for some users.
Form choice: Crack chosen for lower cost per dose and faster onset. Powder chosen for longer, less intense effect.
Most users do not plan long-term dependence, but the neurochemistry makes stopping difficult.
effects: Increased heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature
Depletion of dopamine = anhedonia, depression, cravings
Psychosis: paranoia, hallucinations with heavy use
Cardiovascular: Heart attack, arrhythmia, aortic rupture
Nasal: Damage to septum if snorted
Lungs: "Crack lung" - cough, chest pain, bleeding if smoked
Pregnancy: Preterm birth, low birth weight, developmental risks
Withdrawal: Crash with fatigue, depression, increased appetite, irritability, strong cravings
healthImpact: Acute risks: Overdose can cause cardiac arrest, stroke, hyperthermia, seizures. Risk increases with high doses and mixing with alcohol or other drugs.
Chronic disease: Heart disease, respiratory problems, neurological damage.
Mental health: Anxiety disorders, depression, substance use disorder. Psychosis possible with heavy use.
Infectious disease: If injected, risk of HIV, Hepatitis B/C from shared equipment.
Treatment: No medication specifically approved for cocaine use disorder in most countries. Treatment is behavioral: CBT, contingency management, support groups. Medical care for complications.
socialImpact: Individual: Financial problems, job loss, relationship strain, legal issues.
Family: Conflict, neglect, exposure of children to drug use environments.
Community: Linked to property crime, violence in some drug markets. Strains police, courts, and health services.
Healthcare costs: ER visits, treatment, and long-term care for heart, mental health, and infectious disease.
Stigma: Can prevent people from seeking help.
Workplace: Safety risks in jobs requiring alertness. For transport and other sectors, substance use is a safety and compliance issue.
harmReduction: Talk to a healthcare professional. They can check heart, mental health, and refer to treatment.
Avoid sharing any equipment to reduce infection risk.
If pregnant, seek OBGYN care immediately.
Support: counseling, support groups, and community health services. In Zimbabwe, public hospitals and clinics can refer to mental health and substance use services.
If you or someone is in crisis, experiencing chest pain, severe paranoia, or thoughts of harm, seek emergency medical help immediately.

mechanism: What it is:

Repetition	Ads + news + shows repeat messages. Repetition = belief formation. "Tell-a-vision"

mechanism: How TikTok works technically + psychologically

The For You Page FYP Algorithm: TikTok’s #1 mechanism. Unlike Instagram/Facebook that show friends first, TikTok shows strangers based on behavior.
It tracks: watch time, replays, likes, comments, shares, follows, what you skip in <2 seconds, hashtags, captions, audio, device, location.

Short-form video: 5s to 10min videos. Default is 15-60s. Brain prefers this over long content. Quick reward cycles.
Infinite scroll: No "end". Swipe up = new video instantly. No friction.
Audio-driven: Sounds go viral and everyone uses them. Creates trends in 48 hours.

Dopamine on steroids: Variable ratio reward. You never know if next video will be funny, shocking, hot, useful. Same system as slot machines.
Novelty + Pattern interrupts: Every 3-7 seconds something changes. Cut, text, sound. Keeps attention captured.
Mirroring + Mirror neurons: Watching dances, reactions, POVs makes your brain feel like you’re doing it.
"Just one more" loop: No natural stopping point. Average session is 10.85 minutes but people open app 8x per day.
Identity formation: Algorithm figures out "you" in 200 videos and feeds you that niche: BookTok, GymTok, ZimTok, ChefTok.

mechanism: What it is:
"Algorithmic rage bait" = posts designed specifically to make you angry so you engage. "Outrage content" = news, clips, tweets that trigger moral anger, disgust, or tribal identity.
How the system works:
Mechanism	How it works
Algorithm optimization	TikTok, X, Facebook, YouTube, IG all rank by "engagement". Anger = comments, shares, watch time. So algo pushes angriest content
Dopamine + Cortisol	Outrage gives adrenaline + dopamine. Feels like "doing something". Brain gets hooked on the fight
Moral emotions	Content frames things as "good vs evil". Triggers disgust, righteousness, injustice. Strongest emotions = most shares
Identity threat	Posts attack "your group". Brain treats it like physical threat. You MUST respond
Variable reward	You never know what you’ll be mad about next. Keeps you scrolling for "the next outrage"
Amplification loop	You engage → algo shows you more → you get angrier → you engage more
Creator incentives	Rage bait gets 10x more views than neutral content. So creators learn to make it
The formula: `Trigger + Target + Moral Frame + Call to comment = Viral rage bait`
Example: "Can you BELIEVE this did [shocking thing]. Comment if you agree this is wrong."[group]

Democracy: Makes compromise harder. Everything becomes moral battle.
harmReduction: 24-hour rule: Don’t share/comment when angry. Wait.

Check sources: Rage bait uses out-of-context clips and lies.
